Wheedle

WEE-dul · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To wheedle to use flattery or persistent charming to persuade someone to do something or give something.

The puppy learned to wheedle table scraps out of guests with one well-timed, sorrowful look.

Worked Example

She wheedled her way into an extra day of vacation by reminding her boss, repeatedly and sweetly, of last year's overtime.

Repeated, sweetly delivered reminders to get an extra day off is exactly wheedling.

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

charm

Antonyms

How Strong Is It? — ask → wheedle → beg

ask vs. wheedle

ask vs. wheedle: Ask is a single, plain request; wheedle implies repeated, calculated sweetness aimed specifically at wearing someone down.

beg vs. wheedle

beg vs. wheedle: Beg is more openly desperate and pleading, while wheedle depends on charm and flattery rather than obvious desperation.

Build the Word

The pieces

Put it together

Put it together: Wheedle's exact origin is uncertain, though many dictionaries connect it to a German word meaning 'to wag the tail,' the same eager, ingratiating motion a dog makes when it wants something.

Use the root in a new word: wag

Use the root in a new word: wag: The image behind wheedle -- an eager, tail-wagging kind of persuasion -- gives the word its distinctly warm, ingratiating feel, even though 'wag' itself isn't a direct root.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Wheedle is a warm, slightly playful word for persuasion through charm and persistence, often used for small favors between people who know each other well.
